title: If the light of truth determined assent, faith would be evident; Scripture sets faith against sight
source_text: XXVIII. Deinde, si propria et potissima fidei ratio esset ipsa lux veritatis, quae in rebus credendis cernitur, quaeque mentem ad assensum necessario determinat, fides esset assensus evidens, et dogmata fidei essent evidentia. Siquidem illud est evidens quod luce sua mentem convincit, et cogit ad assensum. At est veluti quoddam scholarum axioma, in Scripturis fundatum, fidem esse habitum mentis inevidentem; quandoquidem Scriptura fidem opponit aspectui: et docet fidem eorum esse quae non videntur.
pass_a_gloss: Next, if the proper and chiefest ground of faith were the very light of truth which is discerned in the things to be believed, and which necessarily determines the mind to assent, faith would be an evident assent, and the dogmas of faith would be evident. Inasmuch as that is evident which by its own light convinces the mind and compels it to assent. But it is as it were a certain axiom of the schools, founded in the Scriptures, that faith is an inevident habit of the mind; inasmuch as Scripture opposes faith to sight: and teaches that faith is of those things which are not seen.
pass_b_english: Next: if the proper and chief ground of faith were the very light of truth discerned in the things to be believed, the light that necessarily determines the mind to assent, then faith would be an evident assent, and the dogmas of faith would be evident. For what is evident is what convinces the mind by its own light and compels assent. But it is almost an axiom of the schools, founded in the Scriptures, that faith is an inevident habit of the mind. Scripture sets faith against sight, and teaches that faith is of things that are not seen.
